![](images/png/fig03_real_vla_survey_taxonomy.png){width="95%"}
:::

::: {#fig-vla-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture**: A representative dataflow. (1) Camera patches receive 2D image-position and camera identifiers alongside language and robot-state tokens; metric depth still requires calibrated evidence. (2) Self-attention mixes the combined token sequence; the colored grid illustrates internal attention weights, not a verified affordance or grasp pose. (3) Discrete autoregressive decoders emit tokens sequentially, whereas continuous decoders generate candidate multi-step chunks ($\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1}$) through one pass or iterative denoising. (4) An independent permission path checks candidate motion against sensed state and modeled limits before actuation. (Synthesized from Brohan et al. [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2], Kim et al. [@kim2024openvla], and Octo Model Team [@octo_2023])." fig-alt="Comprehensive architectural schematic of a Vision-Language-Action foundation model showing spatial patch slicing, 2D positional embeddings, multimodal self-attention weights in an illustrative image grid, discrete vs. continuous action decoders, and an independent proposal boundary."}
![](images/svg/fig03_vla_architecture.svg){width="100%"}
:::

For the mug pick, the model must turn images and instructions into a candidate motion. The dataflow in @fig-vla-taxonomy and @fig-vla-architecture separates that computation into input encoding, a shared representation, and an action decoder, followed by the handoff to independent permission. A token is a vector representing part of an input, such as an image patch; the backbone combines those vectors, and the decoder turns the combined representation into proposed actions. The engineering comparison below follows what each stage stores, transfers, and delivers:

1. **Sensory Ingestion and Spatial Tokenization (The Inputs):**
   A vision transformer (ViT) frontend slices each incoming camera frame into a grid of non-overlapping pixel patches of size $P \times P$ (typically $14 \times 14$ or $16 \times 16$ pixels). Each patch is linearly projected into a vector of width $d$, augmented with 2D spatial sinusoidal positional embeddings, and tagged with a learned camera identifier.

   In an illustrative three-camera configuration (left wrist, right wrist, and an overhead torso mount) capturing $224 \times 224$ images, the image frontend prepares a buffer for each view. Each frame yields $(224 / 14)^2 = 256$ spatial patches. Across three cameras, ingestion injects $3 \times 256 = 768$ visual tokens into the model's sequence on every perceptual step. When concatenated with tokenized natural language commands ($\sim 32$ tokens) and proprioceptive joint state embeddings ($\sim 16$ tokens), the initial context sequence length exceeds $S \approx 800$ tokens. In 16-bit floating-point (FP16) precision ($2\,\text{bytes}$ per element) with hidden dimension $d = 4096$, the initial token embedding matrix alone occupies:
   $$M_{\text{embed}} = S \times d \times 2\,\text{bytes} = 800 \times 4096 \times 2 \approx 6.55\,\text{MB}$$
   Crucially, 2D image coordinates and internal attention patterns do not constitute metric depth: projecting an end-effector into physical 3D space requires calibrated extrinsic camera matrices and depth telemetry.

2. **Multimodal Alignment and Attention (The Backbone):**
   For the illustrative backbone, the token sequence passes through $L = 32$ transformer layers where standard multi-head self-attention computes pairwise token interactions. The cache estimate below assumes full-width keys and values in every layer. While full self-attention incurs quadratic computational complexity ($O(S^2 d)$ FLOPs), at the systems level the Key-Value (KV) cache that retains prior token states for autoregressive context expands linearly ($O(L \cdot S \cdot d)$):
   $$M_{\text{KV}} = 2 \times L \times d \times S \times \text{bytes}$$
   For a 32-layer model with $d = 4096$ using FP16 storage, each context token claims $2 \times 32 \times 4096 \times 2 = 524{,}288\,\text{bytes} \approx 0.524\,\text{MB}$ of KV cache. Reading this KV cache across off-chip DRAM on every token step creates massive memory bus traffic that directly competes with weight streaming. Because memory bus access under Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) is a shared zero-sum resource, fetching tens of megabytes of KV state per step risks starving real-time sensor direct memory access (DMA) buffers. Grouped-query attention (GQA) reduces key-value width by sharing keys and values across query heads; cross-attention can instead limit which retained representations the decoder reads. The saving depends on the architecture and is not implied by action chunking. Furthermore, strong attention weights between language tokens (such as "mug handle") and visual patches do not prove geometric affordance or collision-free clearance; nor does the KV cache track object permanence during physical occlusions. The formal patch-embedding, position-encoding, and attention formulations appear in @sec-appendix-ml-patch-embedding.

3. **Specialized Action Decoders (The Outputs):**
   Instead of generating open-ended conversational text, the final hidden representation $\mathbf{h}_{\text{context}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is routed to specialized action decoders. While vision-language navigation (VLN) models emit topological waypoints or heading rates $(v_t, \omega_t)$ (@fig-vln-navigation), manipulation (VLA) models diverge sharply in how they bridge semantic representations to physical motion:

   Discrete action decoders map each action dimension to a categorical token [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. Sequential token generation can require several model evaluations for one action vector, and discretization limits spatial resolution. Continuous decoders instead emit a trajectory chunk, either directly or through iterative refinement [@chi2024diffusionpolicy; @octo_2023; @black2024pi0]:
   $$\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \mathbf{a}_{t+1}, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}] \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_a} \quad (H = 16\text{--}64\text{ steps})$$
   Here $H$ counts future setpoints and $d_a$ counts values per action. A chunk supplies several requested motions from one sensory context; it does not contain new observations. The runtime comparison therefore depends on how many backbone and decoder evaluations produce the chunk, and how long those evaluations take. @Sec-appendix-ml-multimodal derives discrete tokenization and explains how generative decoders represent alternative demonstrated routes without averaging them into an obstacle.

4. **The Proposal Boundary (Isolation from Actuators):**
   Whether the model is a VLN mobility planner or a VLA manipulation policy, its output is a candidate proposal ($p_t$) on the unprivileged side of the proposal boundary (\ref{dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary}).\index{Unprivileged proposal!proposal boundary} Under the machine model of @sec-boundary-machine-model, the foundation model runs in user space on the application processor and has no path to the pulse-width modulation (PWM) registers or to the current in the motor coils.

   The Brain hands over candidate motion together with the time of the observations that support it. Faster downstream loops track admitted setpoints and regulate motor current using current measurements. A long neural inference cannot suspend those loops or renew old evidence. The full latency budget in @sec-brain-memory-wall prices the path from sensing to actuation; @sec-nervous-invariant-checking develops the independent checking responsibility.

   Proposals reach the permission path through the handoff of @sec-nervous, and the permission path can refuse a hallucinated proposal when independent measurements, modeled limits, and a feasible fallback support that decision.[^fn-math-unprivileged-control]

[^fn-math-unprivileged-control]: **Proposal Boundary**\index{Proposal boundary!unprivileged proposals}: Treating the neural policy as an unprivileged proposal generator isolates stochastic inference from actuator registers. Candidate trajectory setpoints $\mathbf{q}_{\text{ref}}(t)$ are checked on dedicated safety silicon, so proposals that violate modeled actuator limits or keep-out regions can be rejected before any reaches a drive (@sec-nervous-actuation-authority).

::: {#fig-vln-navigation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Topological vision-language navigation**: Embodied navigation architecture executing natural-language spatial instructions. Panoramic visual observations are encoded into perceptual tokens, matched against prompt embeddings, and cross-referenced with a dynamically updated topological navigation graph. The action decoder prunes unreachable nodes and emits metric waypoint offsets $(\Delta x, \Delta y)$ and heading setpoints to guide the chassis along traversable semantic frontiers without requiring an exact geometric prior map. (Adapted from An et al. [@an2023etpnav])." fig-alt="Schematic of topological vision-language navigation showing panoramic observation tokens, topological graph matching, and decoded waypoint offsets and heading setpoints."}
![](images/png/fig03_real_vln_topological_navigation.png){width="95%"}
:::

The representation and decoder determine which data each evaluation must touch. A decoder that retains token history pays for its cache, and a backbone whose weights do not remain on chip pays for new off-chip transfers. These costs make the architecture choice concrete: the mobile manipulator needs both useful task interpretation and timely renewal of motion proposals, but need not assign them to the same model.

## Supply, Freshness, and the Memory Wall {#sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline}

At the pick station the mobile manipulator's arm consumes a new setpoint every few tens of milliseconds, while the mug keeps moving along the conveyor. The selected architecture assigns task interpretation to a large, slower intent model and trajectory renewal to a smaller action-chunk policy. Both propose; a separate real-time path checks and tracks admitted motion. We can test that split by pricing a full weight sweep, comparing it with the required renewal period, and then checking the motion buffer against target drift. The single large-model examples below are alternatives used to expose the trade-off, not changes to the selected machine.

After ingestion (the tokenization of @sec-brain-learned-representations), four stages turn those tokens into proposals (@fig-cognitive-pipeline), and Part III develops each one. Here they matter only for what each hands downstream and how quickly that goes stale.

Perception grounds what it recognizes in metric coordinates relative to the base, so that the mug has a 3D position and orientation (an $SE(3)$ pose) and a graspable handle rather than an abstract semantic label;[^fn-brain-metric-grounding] its output ages from the moment of capture, and @sec-perception turns that age into a contract. Memory carries those estimates through occlusion and must let each one expire when the evidence behind it does (@sec-memory). Intent decomposes a task such as "take the ceramic mug off the conveyor and hand it to the coworker at the packing station" into subgoals, and because the mug moves while the intent model deliberates, it hands the planner a target that expires, an intent lease\index{Intent lease!temporal contract} (@sec-intent-lease). Planning converts that target into candidate setpoints for the base and the arm, the proposals the permission path will judge (@sec-planning). These stages, and the ingestion before them, all run on the application processor and draw on the same memory bus, which is where the machine's cadence is decided.

[^fn-brain-metric-grounding]: **Metric Spatial Grounding**\index{Metric spatial grounding}\index{Special Euclidean group!SE(3) grounding}: While disembodied AI operates over discrete semantic tokens, physical AI must ground those semantics in the Special Euclidean group $SE(3)$, mapping entities to metric distances (meters) and spatial orientations (quaternions) relative to the robot's base coordinate frame. Failing to maintain this metric grounding causes neural policies to emit kinematically impossible Cartesian paths that breach actuator workspace boundaries.

::: {#fig-cognitive-pipeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The physical AI cognitive flow**: Information flows sequentially from physical sensors through Ingestion (tokenization), Perception (spatial geometry and affordances), Memory (persistent world model belief), Intent (deliberative goal leases), and Planning (multi-step action chunking). The flow ends at the proposal boundary, where the permission path evaluates each proposed action against real-time constraints and resources." fig-alt="Horizontal flowchart of the five-stage cognitive pipeline: Ingestion, Perception, Memory, Intent, and Planning, culminating at the proposal boundary."}
![](images/svg/fig03_cognitive_pipeline_horizontal.svg){width="95%"}
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ High-throughput neural inference accelerators are isolated from deterministic cores in @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die.
:::

On an edge robotics system-on-chip (SoC) with unified memory, model weights, sensor transfers, and host computation share memory bandwidth. A policy cannot budget the full bus for itself while assuming that new camera frames arrive without interference. The transfer bound below is therefore a lower bound on evaluation time; the worked comparison later uses an assumed sustained fraction of peak bandwidth. @Sec-placement-resource-contention develops the allocation and loaded tests needed to establish that supply on a shared processor.

### The memory wall {#sec-brain-memory-wall}

When each evaluation streams weights that cannot remain on-chip, memory bandwidth can limit the update cadence of an embodied neural policy even when arithmetic capacity is available. The **memory wall**\index{Memory wall!physical inference} describes the limit imposed when operands cannot reach arithmetic units fast enough to use their available throughput. In physical AI, the consequence is a delayed proposal while the body continues moving.

On-chip static RAM (SRAM) and caches can reuse weights and intermediate state without another external transfer, but only while the working set fits the memory available to that workload. Off-chip LPDDR5 provides much greater capacity through a narrower shared interface. Cache sizes, access latency, and attainable bandwidth depend on the particular processor and allocation; nominal chip-wide capacity does not establish that an action head will remain resident.

To understand the physical consequence of this bandwidth ceiling, consider what happens if a robot attempts to generate continuous motor actions one discrete step at a time through an autoregressive foundation model (such as a multi-billion-parameter VLA model). For a decoder that revisits nonresident weights at each token step, each evaluation streams those weights across the external DRAM bus. In single-token decoding with FP16 weights and request batch size $B = 1$, the dense weight projections become matrix-vector operations ($\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$), yielding an arithmetic intensity, the operations performed per byte transferred, of just $I \approx 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$. The sustained memory bandwidth $B_{\text{mem}}$ and model weight footprint $M_{\text{weights}}$ strictly bound the maximum fresh-evaluation frequency:
$$f \le \frac{B_{\text{mem}}}{M_{\text{weights}}}$$
This bound must use the bandwidth actually available to the policy and the weights it transfers at the selected precision. The worked example below applies it to the mobile manipulator's processor and intent model, before tokenization, multimodal attention, or decoding adds any latency. In single-step autoregressive generation, each action dimension requires predicting additional tokens; if each token revisits off-chip parameters, latency scales linearly with degrees of freedom. Because physical stabilization, joint impedance control, and reflex-level collision avoidance require deterministic update rates of $100\text{--}1000\,\text{Hz}$, the assumed nonresident models cannot supply those control rates. This timing result rules out using that inference path as the fast controller. The separate requirement that learned outputs remain proposals follows from their physical checking obligations, including the timely-but-wrong cases below.

A separate illustrative sequential pipeline shows where additional delay can enter. Its stage ranges are not the selected chunk policy's timing budget:
$$\text{Latency}_{\text{E2E}} = t_{\text{shutter}} + t_{\text{MIPI-DMA}} + t_{\text{vision-encoder}} + t_{\text{policy-backbone}} + t_{\text{action-decoder}} + t_{\text{detokenize}} + t_{\text{CAN-bus}} + t_{\text{FOC-driver}}$$
In this illustrative pipeline, camera shutter exposure integration requires $t_{\text{shutter}} \approx 10\text{--}33\,\text{ms}$, serial MIPI CSI-2 DMA frame grab adds $t_{\text{MIPI-DMA}} \approx 1\text{--}2\,\text{ms}$, Vision Transformer feature extraction takes $t_{\text{vision-encoder}} \approx 15\text{--}30\,\text{ms}$, policy backbone evaluation takes $t_{\text{policy-backbone}} \approx 30\text{--}80\,\text{ms}$, action chunk decoding consumes $t_{\text{action-decoder}} \approx 5\text{--}15\,\text{ms}$, action de-tokenization and safety validation takes $t_{\text{detokenize}} \approx 0.5\text{--}1.0\,\text{ms}$, CAN bus transmission adds $t_{\text{CAN-bus}} \approx 0.5\text{--}2.0\,\text{ms}$, and motor driver current control takes $t_{\text{FOC-driver}} \approx 0.05\text{--}0.1\,\text{ms}$. The rounded total spans $60\text{--}160\,\text{ms}$. These stage ranges describe an example budget, not measured tail latencies or a justified response bound. @Sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses distinguishes those evidence categories; @sec-appendix-systems supplies the memory-wall and roofline background.

This memory wall[^fn-hw-dram-bandwidth] places single-token streaming deep in the memory-bound region of the roofline (@fig-patterson-roofline) [@williams2009roofline]. On the mobile manipulator's application processor it caps the intent model's fresh-evaluation rate, before any vision or decoding work, far below the rate of a joint controller that asks for a new command every millisecond (\ref{nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking}). A model renewed that slowly can say where the arm should go, but it cannot close the loop on moving mass, so it proposes waypoints and a faster loop below it tracks them.

[Single-token decoding at batch size 1]{.heading-3-inline}
Servers can combine independent requests so that a weight matrix multiplies several input vectors at once, reusing fetched weights. A robot waiting for its next action token often has only one such request. Waiting for future observations to form a batch would add delay, and sequentially dependent action tokens cannot all be evaluated at once by an autoregressive decoder. This limits reuse in those projections. It does not make every operation in an embodied model a matrix-vector product. Image patches, multiple camera views, prompt tokens, and parallel action decoders can expose matrix-matrix work within one robot's request. The low-intensity estimate therefore describes the single-token weight sweep, not the complete perception-and-action workload.

[^fn-hw-dram-bandwidth]: **Autoregressive DRAM Bandwidth Saturation**\index{GPU!memory bandwidth wall}: Sequential action tokens can trigger repeated full-model weight traffic when weights are nonresident and the decoder revisits the backbone; cache behavior and hardware determine the actual bandwidth ceiling. Action chunking is one way to reduce the number of full policy evaluations per unit of physical time.

Repeated off-chip transfers also consume memory-system energy. Their power cost depends on the DRAM, controller, access pattern, and transfer rate, so a bandwidth calculation alone does not establish battery drain or actuator heating. The processor's measured power and the chassis thermal path belong in the shared thermal budget of @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.

::: {#fig-patterson-roofline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative embodied roofline**: Arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput using the application processor's dense FP16 GPU ceiling and rounded peak memory bandwidth. Single-token weight streaming can be memory-bound. Chunk length alone does not determine arithmetic intensity; chunked workloads require measured operations and memory traffic. A separate real-time loop executes accepted waypoints between fresh model updates." fig-alt="Illustrative roofline diagram plotting arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput, with a single-token weight-streaming point and a ridge separating memory and compute bounds."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EMBODIED ROOFLINE (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-patterson-roofline
# │ Goal:    show that embodied inference sits far inside the memory-bound regime
# │ Show:    arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput for an edge part
# │ How:     roof from the registry node; the point represents an FP16
# │          matrix-vector weight sweep, excluding other memory traffic
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty, fmt_arithmetic_intensity, fmt_percent, fmt_display_math, check
from mlsysim.core.units import flop, byte

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
soc = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet; the mobile manipulator's application processor
# Select dense FP16 GPU throughput; the aggregate sparse INT8 rating is incompatible.
node = soc.model_copy(update={"compute": soc.compute.model_copy(update={"peak_flops": soc.compute.precision_flops["fp16"]})})
I_TOKEN = 1.0  # category: illustrative; FLOP/byte for a single-token weight sweep

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
peak = node.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
bw = node.memory.bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude
ridge = peak / (bw / 1000)  # FLOP/byte
attainable = lambda ai: min(bw * ai / 1000, peak)

# ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# 2026-09-28: prevent aggregate sparse INT8 TOPS from entering an FP16 roofline.
check(peak == 43, f"Unexpected dense FP16 roof: {peak}")
check(node.compute.peak_flops < soc.compute.peak_flops, "FP16 roof must not use aggregate INT8 TOPS")
check(abs(ridge - 210.7843) < 0.001, f"Unexpected dense FP16 ridge: {ridge}")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
roof_peak_str = fmt_qty(node.compute.peak_flops, unit="TFLOPs/s", precision=0)
roof_bw_str = fmt_qty(node.memory.bandwidth, unit="GB/s", precision=0)
roof_ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(ridge * flop / byte, precision=1)
roof_attainable_str = fmt_qty(attainable(I_TOKEN) * node.compute.peak_flops.units, unit="TFLOPs/s", precision=3)
roof_fraction_str = fmt_percent(attainable(I_TOKEN) / peak, precision=2, style="prose")
roof_ridge_display_math = fmt_display_math(
    rf"I_{{\text{{ridge}}}} = \frac{{\Pi_{{\text{{peak}}}}}}{{\beta_{{\text{{mem}}}}}} = \frac{{{roof_peak_str}}}{{{roof_bw_str}}} \approx {roof_ridge_str}"
)

points = [
    ("Autoregressive VLA\n(single token)", I_TOKEN),
]

# ┌── 5. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = viz.plot_roofline(node)
COLORS = viz.COLORS
ax.set_ylim(peak * 0.0004, peak * 2)  # keep the single-token point on scale
for idx, (label, ai) in enumerate(points):
    y = attainable(ai)
    ax.plot(ai, y, "o", ms=8, color=COLORS["VioletLine"], zorder=11)
    # the lowest point has no room beneath the roof, so its label goes above
    if idx == 0:
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 0.30, y * 4.0), "left", "bottom"
    else:
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 2.4, y * 0.30), "left", "top"
    ax.annotate(
        label,
        xy=(ai, y),
        xytext=pos,
        fontsize=8,
        color=COLORS["VioletLine"],
        ha=ha,
        va=va,
        zorder=11,
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["VioletLine"], lw=0.9),
    )

# the reuse a workload would need before it left the memory-bound regime
ax.annotate(
    f"intensity must reach {ridge:.0f} FLOP/byte\nbefore compute binds",
    xy=(ridge, peak * 0.006),
    xytext=(ridge * 0.30, peak * 0.0012),
    fontsize=8,
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    ha="right",
    zorder=11,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9),
)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The roofline model in @fig-patterson-roofline formalizes the hardware boundary governing embodied inference by plotting attainable computational throughput against **arithmetic intensity** ($I$), defined as:
$$I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes transferred from off-chip memory}}$$
Consider the dense weight projections in single-token autoregressive decoding at batch size 1, each evaluating a matrix-vector product $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$. Counting weight traffic alone, with each weight fetched once for that projection, gives an optimistic intensity estimate; activation and context traffic add further bytes. In 16-bit floating-point precision (FP16, 2 bytes per parameter), each weight participates in exactly one multiply-accumulate operation (2 FLOPs), yielding an arithmetic intensity of:
$$I_{\text{token}} = \frac{2\,\text{FLOPs}}{2\,\text{Bytes}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$$
For the mobile manipulator's Jetson AGX Orin application processor, the dense FP16 GPU Tensor Core ceiling is `{python} roof_peak_str`; the aggregate sparse INT8 rating cannot be used for this FP16 workload. Using the model's rounded peak memory bandwidth of `{python} roof_bw_str`, the hardware ridge point occurs at:
`{python} roof_ridge_display_math`
For this weight-streaming example, $I_{\text{token}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$ is far below `{python} roof_ridge_str`, so memory bandwidth sets the roofline ceiling. Attainable throughput is bounded by $\beta_{\text{mem}} \cdot I_{\text{token}}$, or `{python} roof_attainable_str`, about `{python} roof_fraction_str` of the dense FP16 peak. That ratio is a workload throughput bound, not a measurement of how many cores are idle. If a 7-billion-parameter FP16 decoder emits a 7-DoF action through seven sequential tokens and rereads all weights for each token, the seven transfers alone require nearly $500\,\text{ms}$ at the stated bandwidth. A controller that waits for that entire sequence before each motor update would miss a millisecond deadline; a separate tracking loop must continue between policy evaluations.

Action chunking reduces backbone weight traffic per supplied waypoint when one backbone evaluation supports several future actions. That amortization does not establish an equal increase in arithmetic intensity. Predicting a chunk can add decoder work without repeating the backbone's matrix operations for every waypoint; its roofline position depends on the operations performed and the bytes actually transferred.

For an iterative decoder, each refinement pass adds work on the action head. If the head's weights and intermediate state remain resident on chip, later passes can reuse them without another off-chip transfer. If they do not fit, those passes also add memory traffic. Neither the chunk length nor the number of refinement passes alone determines the whole policy's intensity or attainable throughput. The backbone and head must first be budgeted separately, then combined over the same evaluation interval.

### Action chunking {#sec-brain-action-chunking}

The memory bound limits how often a large model can revise its proposal. A controller can track previously admitted motion between those revisions, but a policy that supplies only one future setpoint leaves little planned motion available while it computes. Predicting a trajectory segment gives the controller a sequence to track without making the next fresh observation arrive sooner.

[Supply rate vs. closed-loop reaction latency]{.heading-3-inline}
To supply dense waypoints despite slow full-model inference, modern physical AI policies employ **action chunking**\index{Action chunking!temporal trajectory} (\ref{dfn-brain-action-chunking}) [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Each chunk then crosses the proposal boundary as one packet, the chunk payload of @sec-nervous-cadences. The transfer saving follows from reusing one evaluation across several outputs.

Predicting a horizon of $H \in [8, 64]$ actions per forward pass spreads the multi-gigabyte DRAM weight streaming cost over $H \times \Delta t_{\text{step}}$ seconds of physical execution. On an edge SoC with $B_{\text{mem}} \approx 204\,\text{GB/s}$ running a 7B FP16 model ($14\,\text{GB}$), generating single-step actions at $50\,\text{Hz}$ would demand $50 \times 14\,\text{GB} = 700\,\text{GB/s}$ of sustained memory bandwidth—exceeding physical bus capacity by over $3.4\times$. An action chunk of $H = 16$ waypoints reduces demanded bandwidth by sixteenfold to $700 / 16 \approx 43.8\,\text{GB/s}$ if one such sweep supplies each full chunk. More frequent replanning, decoder work, and competing memory traffic consume additional bandwidth.

Predicting a sequence also changes how a learned policy uses recent actions, but chunking alone does not establish that the policy attends to the right evidence or recovers from an unfamiliar contact. Those properties depend on training and closed-loop evaluation. The supply calculation establishes only the weight traffic needed for the stated execution schedule.

The selected smaller policy has a separate illustrative schedule. Three quantities distinguish its setpoint supply from the delay before a new observation changes a proposal:

* *Setpoint supply cadence* ($f_{\text{supply}} = 1/\Delta t_{\text{step}} = 50\,\text{Hz}$): The rate at which the trajectory queue delivers discrete waypoints to the joint servo loop.
* *Policy replanning rate* ($f_{\text{replan}} = 20\,\text{Hz}$, period $T_{\text{replan}} = 50\,\text{ms}$): The cadence at which the smaller chunk policy begins an evaluation from fresh sensory frames.
* *Closed-loop reaction latency* ($T_{\text{reaction}} = T_{\text{replan}} + t_{\text{infer}} = 50\,\text{ms} + 40\,\text{ms} = 90\,\text{ms}$): The worst sampling-phase wait plus the assumed inference time until a revised proposal is available, excluding further admission and physical response delay.

In this illustrative schedule, a disturbance immediately after capture can wait up to $90\,\text{ms}$ for a revised learned proposal, before any additional admission and actuation delay. The independent permission path need not wait for that revision: current qualified evidence can trigger a protective response while the policy computes. Its ability to detect the relevant obstacle and complete a feasible response needs its own timing and sensing evidence. Chunking keeps candidate waypoints available; it establishes neither that response nor its deadline.

Chunking policies differ in how they produce the horizon. ACT predicts a chunk directly, whereas a diffusion or flow-matching decoder can refine it iteratively. For the following alternative architecture, assume one backbone pass followed by $K = 10\text{--}16$ refinement steps; those counts are a workload choice, not a property of all chunking policies.

An iterative decoder refines a candidate trajectory over several passes. Generative decoders can represent alternative routes around an obstacle, whereas direct mean-squared-error regression can average those routes into an unusable path. @Sec-appendix-ml-diffusion derives the noise-prediction and flow-matching objectives. For the runtime budget here, the decisive quantities are the number of refinement passes, the working set each pass touches, and whether refinement reevaluates the large backbone.

In the alternative backbone-and-head design, refinement reuses the backbone's context rather than reevaluating its weights on every pass. Whether it also avoids off-chip action-head transfers depends on residency. A $\sim 50\text{M}$-parameter head needs approximately $100\,\text{MB}$ for FP16 weights or $25\,\text{MB}$ for INT4 weights, before intermediate activations. The working set must fit the available cache, not merely the chip's nominal total. A head that does not fit adds traffic on each refinement; one that does fit can still spend time on arithmetic and kernel dispatch. Cache capacity and measured runtime therefore decide whether this alternative helps.

Reducing the number of refinement steps can reduce decoder latency, provided the resulting proposals retain the required task quality. That trade-off needs measurement for the selected policy and processor. It does not remove the time required to encode a fresh observation or evaluate the backbone.

::: {#dfn-brain-action-chunking .callout-definition title="Temporal action chunking"}

***Temporal action chunking***\index{Temporal action chunking!definition}\index{Action chunking!definition} is the policy formulation that predicts an entire horizon of $H$ future continuous actions $\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}]$ in a single neural evaluation or diffusion rollout, amortizing parameter memory transfers across extended physical execution windows.

1.  **Significance**: On a bandwidth-limited device, repeating a full model evaluation for every action can be too slow for millisecond control. Temporal action chunking can reuse a backbone evaluation across multiple waypoints; it does not make fresh observations or policy decisions arrive at the waypoint rate. A downstream controller tracks the accepted trajectory between model updates.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike single-step Markovian policies $\mathbf{a}_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid \mathbf{o}_t)$ that re-evaluate the full neural network at every control step, action chunking deliberately generates multi-step feedforward trajectories, utilizing receding-horizon execution and blending across overlapping chunks to reconcile slow neural deliberation with fast closed-loop control.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Executing action chunks open-loop without continuous temporal smoothing or runtime safety filtering. Without smooth blending across overlapping chunk boundaries, switching between independently generated horizons injects acceleration jumps and torque shocks that excite mechanical gearbox resonances.

:::
For a separate bimanual cable-threading example, consider a 32-step chunk of coordinated 14-DoF joint setpoints on a workcell such as @fig-aloha-manipulator. The longer horizon supplies candidate motion through alignment and insertion; it does not establish successful insertion or smoothness at the next renewal. Those properties depend on the policy, current evidence, and the transition between chunks.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_action_chunk_windows_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Sequence strip illustrating overlapping action chunk horizons of 32 steps with 12-step replanning and temporal ensembling."}

*Overlapping action chunks blend predictions across receding temporal execution windows.*
:::

However, action chunking introduces the problem of **chunk seam continuity**. Because each action chunk is generated independently from rolling sensory observations, the tail of chunk $k$ and the head of chunk $k+1$ may exhibit slight positional and velocity discrepancies. If a controller concatenated these chunks directly, the resulting step-discontinuities in acceleration would inject large jerk ($\dddot{\mathbf{q}}$) into the physical linkages, inducing mechanical shock, acoustic vibration, cycloidal pin wear, and motor overcurrent faults.

To reduce discontinuities between overlapping chunks, systems can implement **temporal ensembling**\index{Temporal ensembling!trajectory smoothing}, blending overlapping trajectory predictions via exponentially weighted averaging:

$$\mathbf{a}_t = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(t, H-1)} w_i \, \mathbf{a}_{t \mid t-i}}{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(t, H-1)} w_i}, \quad w_i = \exp(-m \cdot i)$$

where $\mathbf{a}_{t \mid t-i}$ represents the action predicted for time step $t$ by the action chunk initiated at time $t-i$, and $m > 0$ is a tunable temporal discount factor. The permission path interpolates the blended waypoints below the proposal boundary (@sec-nervous-cadences).

::: {.callout-perspective title="The temporal ensembling jerk trap"}
Exponentially weighted temporal ensembling averages overlapping predictions, but averaging sampled setpoints alone guarantees neither continuous position nor continuous velocity between samples or at chunk boundaries. A downstream interpolator determines those properties. If successive chunks disagree in slope, a controller can receive a step in commanded velocity even when position remains continuous. In joint PD tracking ($\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{K}_p \mathbf{e} + \mathbf{K}_d \dot{\mathbf{e}}$), that velocity jump produces a finite torque step. With derivative gain $K_d = 40\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$ and velocity discontinuity $\Delta \dot{q} = 0.5\,\text{rad/s}$, the derivative term changes by $\Delta \tau = K_d \Delta \dot{q} = 20\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. Dividing by the servo period would instead describe a torque slew rate, not a torque. Abrupt torque changes can excite mechanical resonances or exceed drive limits. Interpolation must match position, velocity, and acceleration at adjoining segments to provide $C^2$ continuity, while enforcing the machine's velocity, acceleration, and torque limits. Smoothness alone does not establish that the requested motion is feasible.
:::

The separation between policy renewal and trajectory tracking determines what an action rate means (@fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline). Discrete decoders generate action tokens sequentially [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. Chunked decoders generate several candidate waypoints from one sensory context, either directly or through iterative refinement [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy; @black2024pi0]. Supplying more waypoints from that context does not refresh the observation on which they depend.

A downstream controller can use current state measurements while tracking admitted waypoints between policy renewals. Its feedback corrects tracking errors within its capabilities; a newly perceived obstacle still requires a timely checking or replanning response. The worked mobile-manipulator budget below therefore distinguishes the interval between fresh policy evaluations from the spacing between waypoints.

::: {#fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Policy renewal and trajectory tracking**: Each fresh policy evaluation produces candidate motion from a sensory context. Overlapping chunks can supply waypoints between renewals, while a downstream controller uses current state feedback to track admitted motion. Additional waypoints do not refresh the policy's evidence. This schematic shows timing relationships, not measured rates or a hardware performance comparison." fig-alt="Three timing rows distinguish fresh observation and policy evaluation events, overlapping candidate chunks, and frequent downstream tracking steps with current state feedback. The shared time axis has no numerical scale."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ POLICY RENEWAL AND TRAJECTORY TRACKING (SCHEMATIC)
# │ Context: @fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline
# │ Goal:    distinguish renewed evidence from supplied waypoints and feedback
# │ Show:    temporal ordering only; coordinates are layout, not measured data
# │ How:     separate observation, chunk, and downstream tracking rows
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

fig, ax, _, _ = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(10, 4.5))
C = viz.COLORS
ax.set_xlim(-3.0, 10.5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 3.4)
ax.axis("off")

rows = [
    (2.6, "Fresh observation\n+ policy evaluation"),
    (1.5, "Candidate chunks\n(subject to permission)"),
    (0.2, "Downstream tracking\n+ current state feedback"),
]
for y, label in rows:
    ax.text(-0.35, y, label, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, color=C["primary"])

for x, chunk_y in [(0.3, 1.75), (4.1, 1.40), (7.9, 1.05)]:
    ax.plot(x, 2.6, "o", color=C["BlueLine"], ms=7)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x + 0.5, chunk_y + 0.14), xytext=(x, 2.48), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=C["primary"], lw=1))

for x, y, end in [(0.8, 1.75, 5.2), (4.6, 1.40, 9.0), (8.4, 1.05, 10.0)]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y - 0.10), end - x, 0.20, facecolor=C["VioletL"], edgecolor=C["VioletLine"], lw=1))
    for j in range(1, int((end - x) / 0.4)):
        xx = x + j * 0.4
        ax.plot([xx, xx], [y - 0.10, y + 0.10], color=C["VioletLine"], lw=0.7)

for j in range(24):
    x = 0.8 + j * 0.4
    ax.plot([x, x], [0.08, 0.32], color=C["GreenLine"], lw=1.3)
ax.annotate("", xy=(10.1, -0.2), xytext=(0.0, -0.2), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=C["primary"], lw=1))
ax.text(10.1, -0.43, "Physical time (schematic)", ha="right", fontsize=9)
ax.text(5.2, 3.2, "A new waypoint is not a new observation", ha="center", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

### Dual proposal pathways in physical inference {#sec-brain-two-proposers}

The single-model alternatives reduce cost per waypoint, but each fresh context still waits for the large backbone. We can now price the selected split between intent and chunk renewal on the warehouse mobile manipulator. Notebook \ref{nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking} applies the memory bound to this split and tests whether chunking alone could give the larger model the required renewal cadence.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-action-chunking-lpddr5
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEMORY WALL AND THE MACHINE'S TWO PROPOSERS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking and the
# │          memory-wall paragraphs that follow it
# │ Goal:    show why the mobile manipulator's intent model cannot renew a
# │          proposal every few tens of milliseconds while its chunk policy can
# │ Show:    98.0 ms per intent-model weight sweep (about 10 Hz before vision);
# │          6.1 ms amortized weight-sweep time per setpoint over H = 16;
# │          0.70 ms per chunk-policy sweep; intent 5 Hz / 160 ms; chunk policy
# │          20 Hz / 40 ms
# │ How:     t_stream = M_weights / (B_peak * dram_efficiency);
# │          tau_step = t_stream / H (calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization)
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_params,
    fmt_memory,
    fmt_bandwidth,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_time,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_display_math,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ActionChunkingLPDDR5:
    """Memory wall and action chunking amortization on the machine's application processor."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = RM.intent_model  # category: chosen (the machine's intent model)
    chunk_model = RM.chunk_model  # category: chosen (the machine's chunk policy)
    soc = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet (application processor)
    params = model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    chunk_params = chunk_model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    bytes_per_param = 2 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen; FP16 weight storage
    bytes_per_param_int4 = 0.5 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen; INT4 alternative
    b_peak = soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet
    soc_mem = soc.memory.capacity  # category: datasheet
    bus_efficiency = RM.dram_efficiency  # category: illustrative; sustained fraction of peak
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen
    chunk_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen
    intent_rate = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    intent_latency = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: illustrative
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    chunk_latency = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 incl. vision
    kv_layers = model.layers  # category: datasheet
    kv_hidden = model.hidden_dim  # category: datasheet
    kv_bytes = 2 * byte  # category: chosen; FP16 key and value storage
    cameras = 3  # category: illustrative; synchronized RGB streams
    patches_per_frame = 256  # category: derived; patch tokens per 224 x 224 frame at P = 14
    context_tokens = 800  # category: illustrative; visual plus language and proprioception tokens per step
    history_window = 5 * second  # category: illustrative; retained visual history
    history_rate = 10 * Hz  # category: illustrative; frames retained per second of history

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weight_mem = memory_from_params(params, bytes_per_param)
    weight_mem_int4 = memory_from_params(params, bytes_per_param_int4)
    res = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=weight_mem,
        memory_bandwidth=b_peak,
        chunk_horizon=chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=bus_efficiency,
    )
    b_sustained = res["b_sustained"]
    t_stream = res["t_stream"]
    f_single = res["f_single"]
    tau_step = res["tau_step"]
    chunk_span = (chunk_horizon * chunk_step).to(millisecond)

    chunk_weight_mem = memory_from_params(chunk_params, bytes_per_param)
    chunk_res = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=chunk_weight_mem,
        memory_bandwidth=b_peak,
        chunk_horizon=chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=bus_efficiency,
    )
    chunk_t_stream = chunk_res["t_stream"]

    visual_tokens = cameras * patches_per_frame
    kv_per_token = (2 * kv_layers * kv_hidden * kv_bytes).to(MB)
    kv_per_frame = (kv_per_token * visual_tokens).to(MB)
    history_frames = round((history_window * history_rate).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    kv_history_visual = (kv_per_frame * history_frames).to(GB)
    kv_per_step = (kv_per_token * context_tokens).to(MB)
    kv_history = (kv_per_step * history_frames).to(GB)
    combined_mem = (weight_mem + kv_history).to(GB)
    combined_ratio = (combined_mem / soc_mem).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(weight_mem.to(GB).magnitude - 14.0) < 0.1, f"Unexpected weight footprint: {weight_mem}")
    check(abs(b_sustained.to(GB / second).magnitude - 142.80) < 0.05, f"Unexpected sustained bandwidth: {b_sustained}")
    check(abs(t_stream.to(millisecond).magnitude - 98.04) < 0.005, f"Unexpected intent sweep: {t_stream}")
    check(abs(f_single.magnitude - 10.20) < 0.05, f"Unexpected single-sweep frequency: {f_single}")
    check(chunk_horizon == 16, f"Unexpected chunk horizon: {chunk_horizon}")
    check(abs(tau_step.to(millisecond).magnitude - 6.13) < 0.01, f"Unexpected per-setpoint sweep time: {tau_step}")
    check(abs(chunk_span.magnitude - 320.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk span: {chunk_span}")
    check(abs(chunk_t_stream.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.700) < 0.0005, f"Unexpected chunk sweep: {chunk_t_stream}")
    check(abs(intent_rate.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected intent rate: {intent_rate}")
    check(abs(intent_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude - 160.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected intent latency: {intent_latency}")
    check(abs(chunk_rate.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk rate: {chunk_rate}")
    check(abs(chunk_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk latency: {chunk_latency}")
    check(t_stream > (1 / chunk_rate), "The intent sweep alone must exceed the chunk period")
    check(chunk_latency < (1 / chunk_rate), "The chunk policy's inference must fit its own period")
    check(kv_layers == 32 and kv_hidden == 4096, f"Unexpected intent-model shape: {kv_layers} x {kv_hidden}")
    check(visual_tokens == 768 and history_frames == 50, f"Unexpected KV scenario: {visual_tokens}, {history_frames}")
    check(abs(kv_per_token.magnitude - 0.524288) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected KV bytes per token: {kv_per_token}")
    check(abs(kv_history_visual.magnitude - 20.13) < 0.01, f"Unexpected visual KV history: {kv_history_visual}")
    check(abs(kv_history.magnitude - 20.97) < 0.01, f"Unexpected context KV history: {kv_history}")
    check(abs(combined_mem.magnitude - 34.97) < 0.01, f"Unexpected weights plus KV footprint: {combined_mem}")
    check(0.45 < combined_ratio < 0.55, f"Weights plus KV must claim about half the SoC memory: {combined_ratio}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(params, precision=0)
    chunk_params_str = fmt_params(chunk_params, precision=0)
    bytes_per_param_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_param.magnitude)
    weight_mem_str = fmt_memory(weight_mem, unit=GB, precision=0)
    weight_mem_int4_str = fmt_memory(weight_mem_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
    chunk_weight_mem_str = fmt_memory(chunk_weight_mem, unit=GB, precision=2)
    b_peak_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_peak, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    b_sustained_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_sustained, unit=GB / second, precision=1)
    dram_eff_pct_str = fmt_percent(bus_efficiency, precision=0, style="prose")
    t_stream_ms_str = fmt_latency(t_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_stream_s_str = fmt_time(t_stream.to(second), 'second', precision=4)
    f_single_str = fmt_frequency(f_single, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=1)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    chunk_step_str = fmt_latency(chunk_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_span_str = fmt_latency(chunk_span, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_step_str = fmt_latency(tau_step, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    chunk_t_stream_str = fmt_latency(chunk_t_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    intent_rate_str = fmt_frequency(intent_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    intent_latency_str = fmt_latency(intent_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    chunk_latency_str = fmt_latency(chunk_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    kv_layers_str = fmt_int(kv_layers)
    kv_hidden_str = fmt_int(kv_hidden, commas=False)
    cameras_str = fmt_int(cameras)
    patches_per_frame_str = fmt_int(patches_per_frame)
    visual_tokens_str = fmt_int(visual_tokens)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_int(context_tokens)
    history_window_str = fmt_time(history_window, 'second', precision=0)
    history_rate_str = fmt_frequency(history_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    kv_per_token_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_token, unit=MB, precision=2)
    kv_per_frame_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_frame, unit=MB, precision=1)
    kv_history_visual_str = fmt_memory(kv_history_visual, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_per_step_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_step, unit=MB, precision=1)
    kv_history_str = fmt_memory(kv_history, unit=GB, precision=1)
    combined_mem_str = fmt_memory(combined_mem, unit=GB, precision=1)
    soc_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory(soc_mem, unit=GB, precision=1)

    t_stream_display_math = fmt_display_math(rf"t_{{\text{{stream}}}} = \frac{{{weight_mem_str}}}{{{b_sustained_str}}} \approx {t_stream_ms_str}")
    f_single_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"f_{{\text{{single}}}} = \frac{{1}}{{t_{{\text{{stream}}}}}} \approx \frac{{1}}{{{t_stream_s_str}}} \approx {f_single_str}"
    )
    kv_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"M_{{\text{{KV}}}} = 2 \times L \times d \times S \times \text{{bytes}} = 2 \times {kv_layers_str} \times {kv_hidden_str} \times S \times 2 \approx {kv_per_token_str} \cdot S"
    )
    tau_step_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{step}}}} = \frac{{t_{{\text{{stream}}}}}}{{H}} = \frac{{{t_stream_ms_str}}}{{{chunk_horizon_str}\text{{ setpoints}}}} \approx {tau_step_str}\text{{ per setpoint}}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking .callout-notebook title="Memory walls, supply, and freshness"}
Can action chunking let a multi-billion-parameter model on an embedded compute module renew proposals as fast as the arm consumes them, or does the machine need a second, smaller proposer?

*1. The single-token memory bottleneck.*
Consider the mobile manipulator's intent model, represented here by the nominal `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.params_str` parameter count of OpenVLA [@kim2024openvla], stored in 16-bit precision (FP16) in the LPDDR5 memory of its application processor, an embedded edge System-on-Chip:

- Weight footprint: $M_{\text{weights}} =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.params_str` params $\times$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.bytes_per_param_str` bytes $\approx$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_str`.
- Rounded theoretical memory bandwidth used in this model: $B_{\text{peak}} =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.b_peak_str`.
- Assumed sustained DRAM bandwidth (`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.dram_eff_pct_str` of peak to model bus scheduling and memory overhead): $B_{\text{sustained}} \approx$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.b_sustained_str`.

Minimum streaming latency to fetch the weights from DRAM across the silicon bus once:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_display_math`

Bandwidth-only upper bound on fresh evaluations when each evaluation streams the full weights:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.f_single_display_math`

Beyond model weights, retained autoregressive context also occupies KV cache. For a hypothetical multi-camera extension of the backbone, when sensory feeds (e.g., `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.cameras_str` $224 \times 224$ RGB streams) are ingested, each video frame contributes hundreds of visual patch tokens (`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.cameras_str` $\times$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.patches_per_frame_str` $=$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.visual_tokens_str` tokens). In the intent model's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_layers_str`-layer transformer with hidden dimension $d =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_hidden_str`, storing the FP16 Key and Value states consumes `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_token_str` per token:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_display_math`
Across one synchronized `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.visual_tokens_str`-token set of camera frames, the KV cache expands by `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_frame_str`. This is a full-width, standard multi-head attention estimate; it is not a measured cache footprint for the published OpenVLA checkpoint.

*2. The action chunking amortization.*
Suppose the intent model itself emitted an action chunk of $H =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_horizon_str` future setpoints ($\Delta t =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_step_str`, spanning `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_span_str`) from each forward pass, instead of one action step per DRAM weight sweep.

- Number of weight memory sweeps: 1 sweep (`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_ms_str`).
- A chunk can reuse one backbone evaluation across $H$ future setpoints.
- Amortized weight-sweep time per setpoint (excluding all other inference work):
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.tau_step_display_math`

*3. The machine's split.*
Amortization spreads one sweep across more setpoints, but it does not make a fresh proposal arrive sooner. Each new chunk from the intent model would still wait for at least one `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_ms_str` sweep, plus tokenization, attention, and decoding. The selected design therefore divides the work between two models. Under its stipulated timing assumptions, the intent model revises the goal at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_rate_str` with `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_latency_str` of inference. A separate `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_params_str`-parameter chunk policy uses ACT as its size reference and is assumed to be adapted to the mobile manipulator. Its `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_weight_mem_str` of weights sweep in `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_t_stream_str`. It proposes base velocity and arm joint targets together at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_rate_str` ($50\,\text{ms}$ replanning period), emitting waypoints spaced at $\Delta t =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_step_str` (a $50\,\text{Hz}$ supply rate), within a `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_latency_str` P99 inference target that includes vision, while the low-level motor drive interpolates and closes current loops at $10\text{--}25\,\text{kHz}$. The intent model's sweep alone exceeds the required renewal period; the chunk policy's leaves room for the remaining work. That is a candidate architecture, not a measured timing result. Loaded execution must establish the inference target, and a percentile target still permits overruns. @Sec-nervous derives an execution lease whose expiration contains a missed renewal.
:::

The `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_ms_str` sweep in \ref{nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking} is a weight-transfer floor. Vision, attention, and decoder work also consume resources; some computation can overlap those transfers, so their durations are not necessarily additive. Lower weight precision could reduce that floor; a fast action head could reduce later decoder work. These alternatives change different terms in the budget. INT4 storage would reduce the nominal weight footprint to `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_int4_str` but needs accuracy validation for contact tasks. A single-model design could instead trade cadence for density without changing weight precision. It would evaluate the `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.params_str` backbone periodically while a lightweight diffusion head denoises candidate trajectories, reusing on-chip data only when its working set fits, supplying dense candidate waypoints from each slower full-model evaluation. Its new-observation rate would still be limited by full inference latency, including vision and decoder work, which is why the mobile manipulator gives renewal to a separate chunk policy instead.

Retained context adds to the pressure the notebook began to measure. Counting language and proprioception tokens along with the visual patches raises each step to $S \approx$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.context_tokens_str` tokens, so at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_token_str` of FP16 key-value state per token each observation step adds `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_step_str` of KV cache. Retaining an unpruned `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.history_window_str` historical context window at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.history_rate_str` would yield `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_history_str` of KV cache. This hypothetical history exceeds the published OpenVLA checkpoint's configured context window; the calculation exposes the storage cost of such an extension, rather than claiming that the checkpoint supports it. Combined with the intent model's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_str` of weights, this example claims `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.combined_mem_str`, about half of the application processor's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.soc_mem_gb_str` before runtime overhead, memory that perception, mapping, and the chunk policy also need. Even where memory capacity permits, reading a large cache is further traffic on that same bus (@sec-placement-resource-contention). Bounding retained history therefore serves both capacity and timely renewal. Spatial pooling or cross-attention can reduce context traffic; fixed-horizon action output does not by itself bound the observation history retained by the backbone.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-conveyor-chunk-sizing
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONVEYOR CHUNK SIZING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the conveyor-pick paragraph in @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline
# │ Goal:    size the chunk the mobile manipulator's arm executes against the
# │          mug's drift on the moving conveyor
# │ Show:    the 219 ms tracked evidence horizon; the 90 ms open-loop span
# │          (50 ms replanning period plus 40 ms inference) inside it; the
# │          16-step, 320 ms chunk as a supply buffer that would breach the
# │          grasp tolerance if executed to its end
# │ How:     tau_ev = sqrt(2 (r_tol - e_0) / a_slip); open-loop span = 1/f_chunk +
# │          t_chunk; drift = a_slip T^2 / 2
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ConveyorChunkSizing:
    """Chunk supply and evidence horizon for the mug on the moving conveyor."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_conv = AISLE.v_conveyor  # category: illustrative
    a_slip = AISLE.a_conveyor_slip  # category: illustrative
    r_tol = AISLE.grasp_tolerance  # category: chosen
    e_0 = AISLE.grasp_initial_error  # category: illustrative
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    chunk_latency = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative
    chunk_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_ev = ((2 * (r_tol - e_0) / a_slip) ** 0.5).to(millisecond)
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    open_loop = (chunk_period + chunk_latency).to(millisecond)
    h_min = math.ceil((open_loop / chunk_step).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    chunk_span = (chunk_horizon * chunk_step).to(millisecond)
    drift_open_loop = (0.5 * a_slip * open_loop**2).to(millimeter)
    drift_full = (0.5 * a_slip * chunk_span**2).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_conv.to("m/s").magnitude - 0.20) < 1e-9, f"Conveyor speed drifted: {v_conv}")
    check(abs(tau_ev.magnitude - 219.09) < 5e-3, f"Tracked evidence horizon drifted: {tau_ev}")
    check(abs(chunk_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk period drifted: {chunk_period}")
    check(abs(open_loop.magnitude - 90.0) < 1e-9, f"Open-loop span drifted: {open_loop}")
    check(open_loop < tau_ev, "The open-loop span must sit inside the evidence horizon")
    check(h_min == 5, f"Minimum supply horizon drifted: {h_min}")
    check(chunk_horizon == 16, f"Chunk horizon drifted: {chunk_horizon}")
    check(abs(chunk_span.magnitude - 320.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk span drifted: {chunk_span}")
    check(chunk_span > tau_ev, "The full chunk must outlast the evidence horizon (buffer, not plan)")
    check(e_0 + drift_full > r_tol, "Executing the whole chunk open-loop must breach the grasp tolerance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_conv_str = fmt_velocity(v_conv, unit="m/s", precision=2)
    a_slip_str = fmt_acceleration(a_slip, precision=2)
    r_tol_str = fmt_length(r_tol, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    e_0_str = fmt_length(e_0, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    tau_ev_rounded = round(tau_ev.magnitude) * millisecond  # whole-ms display; the guard pins 219.09 ms
    tau_ev_str = fmt_latency(tau_ev_rounded, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_latency_str = fmt_latency(chunk_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    open_loop_str = fmt_latency(open_loop, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    h_min_str = fmt_int(h_min)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    chunk_step_str = fmt_latency(chunk_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_span_str = fmt_latency(chunk_span, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    drift_open_loop_str = fmt_length(drift_open_loop, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    drift_full_str = fmt_length(drift_full, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

In the illustrative conveyor calculation, the mobile manipulator's arm takes the mug from a conveyor moving at `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.v_conv_str`, and each chunk must be executed without letting the mug drift out of reach. Untracked, the belt's steady motion would use up the margin $r_{\text{tol}} - e_0$ between the grasp tolerance and the handle estimate's initial error $e_0$ within the freshness deadline $e_{\max}/v_{\max}$ of @sec-body-measurement-freshness, with $e_{\max} = r_{\text{tol}} - e_0$. A tracker that follows the mug removes that steady motion, but residual slip can still accelerate the target at `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.a_slip_str`, so a segment executed open-loop for a time $T$ drifts by $\frac{1}{2} a_{\text{slip}} T^2$. Added to the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.e_0_str` initial error $e_0$, that drift reaches the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance after the tracked evidence horizon $\tau_{\text{ev}} = \sqrt{2 (r_{\text{tol}} - e_0) / a_{\text{slip}}} \approx$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str`. The chunk policy replans every `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_period_str` and is assumed to finish within `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_latency_str`. Before additional handoff delays, this schedule gives a maximum evidence age at replacement of `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop_str` and residual drift of `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.drift_open_loop_str`, within the tracked evidence horizon. An overrun ends this assumption; the independent lease limits continued execution.

That open-loop span also sets the minimum supply, because a chunk shorter than `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.h_min_str` setpoints would leave the arm waiting for its successor. The machine's chunk carries `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_horizon_str` setpoints at `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_step_str` spacing, `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span_str` of motion, longer than the tracked evidence horizon; executed open-loop to its end, it would drift `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.drift_full_str`, past the tolerance. The unexecuted tail is therefore a supply buffer, not permission to finish the predicted trajectory. If renewal stops, any further prefix remains eligible only while its evidence and active execution lease remain valid. @Sec-nervous-cadences derives the lease and accounts for the handoff delays before that buffer runs out. Overlapping chunks and temporal ensembling then blend the executed motion across each renewal.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Bounded action chunk proposals are filtered against forward-invariant barriers in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.
:::

Under the stated assumptions, the conveyor calculation supplies the quantities needed to connect cognition to physical permission. One chunk covers `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span_str` of motion, a new chunk takes up to `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_latency_str`, and the evidence stays within the stated grasp tolerance for about `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str`. The Nervous System must combine these proposer limits with the body's measured limits to establish its handoff record. That requires more information than a trajectory tensor alone. Timely delivery and usable evidence bound how long a proposal can remain eligible; they do not establish that the proposed grasp was correct.

### Information the proposer must supply {#sec-brain-proposer-information}

The conveyor budget gives each payload field a physical purpose. The receiver needs the candidate motion, the capture time from which its evidence ages, and the conditions limiting its validity. The following illustration groups that information with delivery metadata; it is not a new evidence record in the book's record chain. @Sec-nervous owns the execution header and the handoff record that combine this supply with the body's limits.

::: {#dfn-brain-proposal-contract .callout-definition title="The proposal record"}

***The Proposal Record***\index{Proposal Record!definition}\index{Proposal contract!definition}\index{Proposal boundary!contract schema} ($\mathcal{P}$) is a typed candidate-motion payload sent from the unprivileged Brain to the real-time Nervous System. The payload illustration here packages candidate trajectory setpoints, capture timestamps, evidence validity horizons, and provenance metadata for independent verification before execution permission is granted:
$$\mathcal{P} = \langle t_{\text{capture}}, t_{\text{valid}}, H, \Delta t, \mathbf{Q}_{1:H}, \dot{\mathbf{Q}}_{1:H}, \mathbf{X}_{1:H}, \mathbf{g}_{1:H}, \text{model\_id}, \text{lease\_id}, \hat{p}, \text{crc} \rangle$$

1. **Significance**: Capture timestamps and validity claims let the receiver compare candidate motion with independently established freshness and calibration requirements before admission.
2. **Distinction**: This candidate payload describes requested motion. It is neither execution permission nor the handoff evidence record; the receiver must check its claims against current state and established limits.
3. **Common pitfall**: Omitting observation timestamps or validity horizons, causing downstream controllers to execute delayed proposals computed from obsolete scene states.

:::

The fields in @tbl-03-proposal-record-schema illustrate the information needed to interpret a candidate trajectory, rather than prescribing a second wire format. The proposer supplies trajectory and observation information. Validity claims require supporting evidence, while the receiver applies the separately established execution lease. A `lease_id` associates the request with that permission process; it does not let the proposer grant itself authority. The header and handoff contract in @sec-nervous specify delivery, admission, and expiration.

| Field         | Type                        | Unit                    | Systems Semantics and Verification Rule                                                                            |
|:--------------|:----------------------------|:------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `t_capture`   | `uint64_t`                  | $\text{ns}$             | Hardware timestamp of oldest sensory observation conditioning the proposal.                                        |
| `t_valid`     | `uint64_t`                  | $\text{ns}$             | Monotonic time after which proposal expires ($\le t_{\text{capture}} + \tau_{\text{ev}}$).                         |
| `horizon_H`   | `uint16_t`                  | count                   | Number of prospective trajectory setpoints ($H = 16\text{--}64$).                                                  |
| `delta_t`     | `uint32_t`                  | $\mu\text{s}$           | Temporal interval between consecutive waypoints ($\Delta t = 20\,000\,\mu\text{s} \implies 50\text{ Hz}$).         |
| `q_traj`      | `float32[H][D]`             | $\text{rad}$            | Candidate joint trajectory array across $D$ degrees of freedom.                                                    |
| `q_dot_traj`  | `float32[H][D]`             | $\text{rad/s}$          | Velocity setpoints; checked for continuity when adjoining chunks meet.                                             |
| `x_cartesian` | `position + orientation[H]` | $\text{m}, \text{quat}$ | End-effector target poses; verified against workspace keep-out boundaries.                                         |
| `gripper_cmd` | `float32[H]`                | $[0, 1]$                | Gripper closure target; evaluated against grasp force and slip limits.                                             |
| `model_id`    | `uint32_t`                  | identifier              | Identifier resolving to the model architecture, weights checkpoint, and calibration profile.                       |
| `confidence`  | `float32`                   | $[0, 1]$                | Model reported confidence $\hat{p}$; interpreted using calibration evidence from observed outcomes.                |
| `lease_id`    | `uint64_t`                  | identifier              | Identifier linking the proposal to a time-limited permission record; the handoff protocol follows in @sec-nervous. |
| `crc32`       | `uint32_t`                  | checksum                | Integrity checksum protecting shared-memory ring buffer payload.                                                   |

: **Illustrative proposal payload fields**: Candidate-motion information and associated metadata. The execution header and handoff record are defined in @sec-nervous; this illustration adds no separate qualification record. {#tbl-03-proposal-record-schema tbl-colwidths="[18,14,14,54]"}

↪ Zero-copy proposal passing between the Brain and the Nervous System relies on the lock-free buffers analyzed in @sec-nervous-cadences.
